Gravity.title: Universal Law of Gravitation
Gravity.description: All bodies with mass attract each other. What makes that force stronger? Experiment, make a prediction and discover Newton’s law.
Gravity.diagramNote: Arrows indicate mutual attraction. Sizes, separation and arrows are illustrative, not to scale.
Gravity.tinyForce: N means newton, the unit of force. This laboratory uses large masses and distances in kilometres; calculations convert everything to kilograms and metres.
Gravity.challenge_oneMass: 1. What if you double one mass?
Gravity.challenge_bothMasses: 2. What if you double both masses?
Gravity.challenge_distance: 3. What if you double the distance?
Gravity.baseline: Each challenge uses the same baseline: two masses of 40 × 10¹² kg with centres 8 km apart. Checking applies the challenge values.
Gravity.predict: How do you think the force will change?
Gravity.four: It becomes four times as strong
Gravity.quarter: It becomes one quarter as strong
Gravity.feedback_oneMass: Doubling one mass doubles the force. The other mass and the distance stay unchanged.
Gravity.feedback_bothMasses: Each mass contributes a factor of two: 2 × 2 = 4. The force is four times its initial value.
Gravity.feedback_distance: Distance is squared. Doubling it divides the force by 2² = 4, leaving one quarter.
Gravity.feedbackNote: This explanation describes the challenge values. You can keep experimenting with the controls.
Gravity.summary: You explored all three relationships: more mass means more force; more distance means less force. Try your own combinations!
Gravity.tutorIntro: The tutor uses current values and your latest prediction. Ask for an explanation or an example to understand the result.
Gravity.thinking: The tutor is preparing your explanation…
Gravity.notConfigured: The tutor is not available yet. You can still use the laboratory and challenges.
Gravity.tutorError: Could not get an explanation. Try again; the laboratory still works.
Gravity.staleReply: You changed the experiment. Ask again to use the new values.
Gravity.aiNote: AI explanations may contain errors. Force values are calculated using Newton’s law.
Gravity.formulaIntro: Force increases with each mass and decreases with the square of the distance. This relationship is written as:
Gravity.formulaSpoken: Force equals G times mass one times mass two, divided by distance squared.
Gravity.forceDefinition: Attractive force in newtons (N). Both bodies experience equal forces in opposite directions.
Gravity.constantDefinition: The gravitational constant: 6.67430 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg². Its value is very small.
Gravity.massDefinition: The two masses in kilograms (kg). Increasing either increases the force.
Gravity.distanceDefinition: Distance between centres in metres (m). The square explains why separating bodies reduces the force so much.
Gravity.modelNote: Simplified model: non-overlapping spherical bodies treated as point masses at their centres. We show force, not a trajectory simulation.
Gravity.nextTopic: What changes with a third body?
Gravity.experimentHint: Change one value at a time and observe the force. Masses are in × 10¹² kg and distance in km. You can reset values at any time.
Gravity.challengesHint: Answer one challenge at a time. Check your prediction to see the result and an explanation.
Gravity.formulaHint: Connect what you observed with the formula. You do not need to memorise it.
Gravity.optionalHelp: Need help? Open the AI tutor
Gravity.visualDescription: Two masses attract with equal and opposite forces. Arrows show direction only; their length does not measure force. Sizes and separation are illustrative.
Gravity.stageNote: Illustrative sizes · fixed bodies to compare force
Gravity.takeaway: More mass, more attraction. Twice the distance, one quarter of the force.
Gravity.introTitle: Everything with mass attracts something else.
Gravity.introParagraph: Objects do not need to touch. Gravity acts at a distance, between you and Earth, between two asteroids or between stars.
Gravity.introNewton: Newton expressed it with a single formula: attraction increases with mass and decreases rapidly as bodies move farther apart.
Gravity.legendMasses: The masses of the two bodies
Gravity.formulaInteractionHint: Hover, tap or focus a symbol to highlight its definition. Click to keep it highlighted.
Gravity.calculatorHint: Enter values: the result and laboratory update automatically. G is constant.
Gravity.calculatorInvalid: Enter a value within range and with the allowed step: whole masses and distance to one decimal. The last valid calculation remains until then. Leaving the field restores its last valid value.
Gravity.inlineFormulaHint: Edit m₁, m₂ and r directly in the formula. The result and laboratory update when you enter valid values.
Gravity.invalidFieldValue: Use a value from {min} to {max}, in steps of {step}.
Gravity.resultPending: Enter both masses and the distance to calculate F.
Gravity.definitionCalculatorHint: Enter values in the mass and distance cards. G is fixed. Calculating also applies the values to the laboratory.
Gravity.automaticCalculatorHint: Fill in three of the four values: the fourth is calculated automatically. The result is locked and updates when inputs change. Reset to choose another unknown.
Gravity.positiveValue: Enter a number greater than zero.
Gravity.threeValuesNeeded: Enter three positive values to obtain the fourth.
Gravity.numericalError: The values are too large or small to calculate a reliable result. Try other values.
Gravity.outsideLabRange: Valid result outside the laboratory’s visual range (masses of 10–100 × 10¹² kg and distance of 5–20 km). The previous experiment is preserved.
Gravity.massEquationSpoken: Unknown mass equals force times distance squared, divided by G times the other mass.
Gravity.distanceEquationSpoken: Distance equals the square root of G times both masses divided by force.
Gravity.clickToEditFormulaHint: Click F, m₁, m₂ or r² to enter a value. On blur, it shows the value or its symbol if empty. Three inputs calculate the fourth; reset to choose another unknown.
Gravity.principle_mass_description: Double one mass and attraction doubles too. The effects of the two masses multiply.
Gravity.principle_distance_description: Double the separation and force is divided by four. Triple it and force is divided by nine.
Gravity.principle_mutual_description: The two bodies experience equal and opposite forces. The lighter body accelerates more: a = F/m.
Gravity.tryChallengeTitle: What if you move the bodies twice as far apart?
Gravity.tryChallengeDescription: Set the distance to 5 km, then to 10 km, without changing the masses. Compare the force: it should fall to one quarter.

ThreeBody.title: The Three-Body Problem
ThreeBody.description: Explore the motion of three bodies under gravity.
